subtopic: EXTENSION OF PENSION PROVISIONS AND DISTRIBUTION OF FINES AND PENALTIES
speechtext:
I was going to say a
word on this subject when we reached sections 4 and 5 of the bill. I believe this is a continuation of a new policy which seems to militarize the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. During the past three years it seems to have been the custom to consider members of the force as military men. Their years of service in the militia count, and in many other ways they have become to some extent what people would call militaristic. I think it would be a great mistake if that was the spirit that was to prevail in the end. The police force of Canada or of any country should be kept as far away as possible from the military end of the national organization. They should act in quite a different way, but I have heard it said during the last two or three years that military methods were being introduced in the mounted police, and I am certainly not in accord with that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: EXTENSION OF PENSION PROVISIONS AND DISTRIBUTION OF FINES AND PENALTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in reply
to my hon. friend from Quebec East I entirely agree with him that the force is not a military force, should not be so treated and should not be so considered. It was established as a police force and in order to keep it as a police force it was thought better in the early days to attach it to the Department of Justice rather than to any other department, in order that it might remain purely and simply a police force, and there it is at the present day. I know of no military operation or anything in the nature of a military operation that the force has ever been called upon to perform unless in connection with the northwest rebellion of 1885. The training is police training; the whole

Mounted, Police Act
idea of the training and of the system is to keep the force distinctly a police force. If my hon. friend from Quebec East would mention some of the instances to which he refers I will make inquiry into them.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PENSION PROVISIONS AND DISTRIBUTION OF FINES AND PENALTIES
speechtext: Only recently the newspapers carried a report of a complaint that was made by a barrister in Halifax, Nova Scotia, a Mr. Molnnes, who complained very bitterly of the treatment that was meted out to one of the witnesses of the accused, I forget which, in the recent cases involving charges of evasion of the customs laws. My recollection is that very grave charges of undue exercise of third degree methods were made against the officers of the police. I think it might be interesting to the house to know to just what extent the Canadian military forces or the Canadian police are entitled to use third degree methods. Just because they are in effect in other countries, have we decided that we are going to carry on this very un-British practice of persecuting or tormenting people in order to make them confess or make statements to the police which they otherwise would not make? I think it might be informative to the house if the minister would give us a statement as to the authority of the mounted police in matters of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: EXTENSION OF PENSION PROVISIONS AND DISTRIBUTION OF FINES AND PENALTIES
speechtext:
I may say in reply to
my hon. friend who has just taken his seat that I would resent just as much as he does, or anyone else would, any insinuation that what are knowm as third degree methods were employed by the police. I have heard statements made and I have made inquiries in regard to specific cases, and I am satisfied that there is no foundation for such charges. The police are instructed otherwise. They are a police force. I am aware that in some parts of the world what are called third degree methods are in vogue and it may be in some municipal forces in Canada, although I do not know that; but positive instructions are issued to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police that no third degree methods are permissible and if any member of the force seeks to practise them I only wish it would be reported.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PENSION PROVISIONS AND DISTRIBUTION OF FINES AND PENALTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on the
question of the conduct of the mounted police in the matter of the use of third degree methods, I brought a case to the attention of the Solicitor General last session, I think it was, and the Solicitor General promised to make an investigation. Apparently an investigation was made in an ex parte manner, if I may use the term, and the report was sent in to the department that there was no foundation for the statement. I repeat here to-day that there is foundation, that there was no proper investigation held, and I want now to go one step further.
Another case arose in my town where the mounted police, the same ones I complained of before, put a prisoner, the accused, through the third degree in the worst manner possible. The young man was accused of manslaughter. He was supposed to have been driving at night and to have struck an individual and not to have stopped when the accident took place. The man died and this young man was arrested by the mounted police. He was not put in gaol but taken before the mounted police and questioned. The officers who questioned him were not the ones who took what purported to be his confession, and those officers who questioned him told him that the oar they had examined had Wood on it and that one of the mudguards in front was broken and that a piece of it was found on the road, which was an absolute lie. I was present in court, and one of the mounted police was asked whether he was a party to the questioning. He said no. Then he was asked, "Were you a party to examining this car?" He said yes. Then he was asked, "llf a confrere, a brother policeman of yours, made the statement that there was blood on that oar and that one of the mudguards was
Mounted Police Act

broken, would you say that he told the truth?" "No," he said, "I would say he lied." I was present in the court and heard this. The young man, he was just a young boy of eighteen or nineteen, had gone over that road the night of the accident but said he had never struck anybody so far as he could ascertain. He did in a matter of confession, after this third degree questioning, after he was told there was blood on his car, after he was told the mudguard was broken, say, "I may have struck somebody lying down on the road but I certainly did not knock a man down." While the trial was going on before the supreme court Mr. Justice Le Blanc refused to allow this purported confession to be put in evidence because the policeman who had questioned the prisoner was not the one who was in court and he could not be found, and for that reason the purported confession was not allowed in evidence.
What happened? The jury cleared this young man but the police brought a charge against him for violent and dangerous driving, whatever the term is, before a police magistrate, and this purported confession that he had made to the police was allowed in evidence before the police magistrate and the young man was fined $50 and costs for vicious or violent driving.
I am making this statement on my honour as a member o>f the house. The third degree was applied to that young man, and I do not want to see any more investigations like the one that was held by Captain Salt, who is head of the police of the province. Captain Salt on that occasion came all the way from Fredericton to Bathurst, and he assisted at that inquiry by the police, and then went home. After Captain Salt had gone back to Fredericton the young man was taken before two policemen who had not questioned him but who knew the questions that he had been asked and the answers he gave, and they induced him to make a sort of confession which was used against him. Now if this is going to foe allowed to go on, the worth of the mounted police will be at an end. Their authority will be no longer any good.
Take the case in the province of Quebec to which reference has been made. In that instance there was almost a forced confession, and I do not care what police force was involved in it; I am discussing the question of third degree methods. The supreme court refused the evidence. Now I submit that if the mounted police or any other police force are going to use methods of that kind to get evidence, then bringing the criminals before

the court, you cannot expect to get convictions. No justice of the court, made aware of the circumstances under which such evidence is obtained, is going to allow such confessions to go in. There is a method of obtaining evidence and the police are paid for doing that work; but they are not paid for this third degree business.
Referring to the case mentioned by the hon. member for Quebec South, the Mclnnes case, let me call the attention of the attorney general to another case-and 'perhaps I am out of order in discussing it inasmuch as it is before the courts now for preliminary examination. A lady and her daughter have produced evidence-I saw the affidavit myself -showing that the mounted police went to their house and demanded to know where her husband was. Apparently she did not know at the time, whether he was in the city or not and they demanded that she go to the bank and open the safety deposit box in the name of her husband and herself. She refused, and the policeman who was there, accompanied by another told her that if she did not appear at the bank at 10 o'clock the next morning he would break the box open with an axe. At 10 o'clock the next morning she was there, and under threats she opened the deposit box and the police took out of the box all the papers belonging to these people. When the matter came up before the court the other day in Montreal, and this question of third degree methods was involved, the lawyers prosecuting refused to file the documents taken out of that box, in order to prevent this lady from going on the stand with her daughter and giving evidence. The policemen denied the affair and the court decided that the affidavits would not be taken because the individuals could be produced. The defence offered to produce the individuals and brought them there at two o'clock in the afternoon. In the afternoon at two o'clock the prosecuting attorneys refused to file the papers taken out of the box, so that these ladies could not be put on the stand as witnesses to prove that the mounted police had attempted by third degree methods to procure the documents. I would direct these cases to the attention of the attorney general. I have seen the affidavits in the Montreal case, and I was present in the court and followed the whole proceedings in the case that came up in Bathurst, so that I know that third degree methods have been applied. I would ask therefore for an investigation not by Captain Salt in Fredericton, the head of the mounted police of New Brunswick, but by a person sent from the Department

Mounted Police Act
of Justice in Ottawa, someone who will not play favourites with anyone but will carry out a fair and square investigation of the facts. And I will be prepared to produce witnesses because I do not want an ex parte investigation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: EXTENSION OF PENSION PROVISIONS AND DISTRIBUTION OF FINES AND PENALTIES
speechtext: I should be glad to grant the request of my hon. friend in regard to the New Brunswick case which he has mentioned and which has not been brought to my attention before.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PENSION PROVISIONS AND DISTRIBUTION OF FINES AND PENALTIES
speechtext: No, I did not bring it to your attention.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: EXTENSION OF PENSION PROVISIONS AND DISTRIBUTION OF FINES AND PENALTIES
speechtext: The hon. member makes a complaint as to some confession which was allegedly taken by third degree methods. My idea of third degree methods is that they are methods whereby men are cajoled and threatened and tortured and exhausted, as a result of which statements are obtained from them.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PENSION PROVISIONS AND DISTRIBUTION OF FINES AND PENALTIES
speechtext: I gave you cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: EXTENSION OF PENSION PROVISIONS AND DISTRIBUTION OF FINES AND PENALTIES
speechtext: I am satisfied that nothing of the kind has taken place.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PENSION PROVISIONS AND DISTRIBUTION OF FINES AND PENALTIES
speechtext: I am satisfied it has.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: EXTENSION OF PENSION PROVISIONS AND DISTRIBUTION OF FINES AND PENALTIES
speechtext:
We have no particulars of it yet. But it is common in every police system in the world, I think, to question witnesses or supposed criminals before they are arrested. It is the method of doing it that is sometimes called the third degree, but the mere fact of questioning transpires, I think, in every important criminal case in this country. If confessions are obtained by threats or promises the court very properly rules them out. The court in New Brunswick, according to my hon. friend's statement, did rule out the confession against this man who was charged, but subsequently when the matter came before the magistrate's court, he was fined $50 for reckless driving or something of the kind. If there is any complaint in regard to that, it cannot be made against the mounted police but against the judiciary or the magistrates of New Brunswick. We do not enforce the criminal laws in any province; the provinces enforce them, and if the magistrate has made a mistake there is recourse and appeal can be taken against his decision under the laws of New Brunswick. So far as I can see, however, no wrong has been done, nor has any injury followed. But to gratify my hon. friend, because he is always very positive in his statements, I will have an investigation made by someone outside the establishment in the province of New Brunswick. I will have it done by someone from Ottawa. I do not know about the Montreal case, and if I
did I would not discuss it now, because it is before the courts. But on the statement that has been made, I see nothing to complain of in the conduct of the mounted police.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PENSION PROVISIONS AND DISTRIBUTION OF FINES AND PENALTIES
speechtext: Surely the Minister of Justice does not mean to say that there is nothing wrong in the conduct of the mounted police, from the statement I have made. Will he approve of the mounted police lying to an individual-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: EXTENSION OF PENSION PROVISIONS AND DISTRIBUTION OF FINES AND PENALTIES
speechtext: No.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PENSION PROVISIONS AND DISTRIBUTION OF FINES AND PENALTIES
speechtext: -and telling him that there was blood on the car when there was not, telling him the mudguard was broken when it was not, in order to induce that individual to admit that he must have struck the man? He lied to him, misrepresenting the whole situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: EXTENSION OF PENSION PROVISIONS AND DISTRIBUTION OF FINES AND PENALTIES
speechtext: That is the case I promise to investigate.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PENSION PROVISIONS AND DISTRIBUTION OF FINES AND PENALTIES
speechtext: Then I will ask the minister this. When the investigation takes place, I will ask him not to have it held until I am at home after the session.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: EXTENSION OF PENSION PROVISIONS AND DISTRIBUTION OF FINES AND PENALTIES
speechtext: I will agree to that too.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PENSION PROVISIONS AND DISTRIBUTION OF FINES AND PENALTIES
speechtext: I ask that because I want to push this thing to the limit.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: EXTENSION OF PENSION PROVISIONS AND DISTRIBUTION OF FINES AND PENALTIES
speechtext: And if the hon. member will write me a letter giving names and dates, I shall have the preliminaries prepared, awaiting his return home.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PENSION PROVISIONS AND DISTRIBUTION OF FINES AND PENALTIES
speechtext:
Here is another thing about the conduct of the police. I hold a return from the Department of National Revenue in connection with the seizure of a vessel; I will not discuss that now; I will discuss the question fully when it comes up in the estimates. But I inquired what instructions were given the mounted police in connection, first, with the destruction of the vessel, and secondly, with the destruction of the liquor seized on board. The Department of National Revenue replied that they gave definite instructions for the destruction of the vessel and the destruction of the cargo. I then asked whether instructions were issued by the Department of National Revenue for the disposal of the stores found on board this vessel, and, if so, what those instructions were. The answer is, "No specific instructions." Now I want to know this. If the police received no specific instructions to destroy the stores of the ship, were they justified in taking those stores which had been seized on board the ship and carrying them to a private house of one of the mounted police, whose family were living there, and
Mounted Police Act

who had custody of those stores? They took them without specific instructions to take the ship's stores, consisting of pork, biscuits, flour and other provisions amounting to 8600. They took these stores down to the shore, poured gasoline over them and destroyed them in the presence of hundreds of people who were on relief and who were pleading to get the stores rather than to see them destroyed. The department replied to me that no specific instructions were issued. I want to know whether the mounted police were justified in destroying those stores in that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: EXTENSION OF PENSION PROVISIONS AND DISTRIBUTION OF FINES AND PENALTIES
speechtext: I would very much prefer if cases of this kind were brought to my attention on the estimates of the mounted police and not on this bill. I would then have the commissioner in front of me and be able to give the information.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PENSION PROVISIONS AND DISTRIBUTION OF FINES AND PENALTIES
speechtext: I will bring the matter up then. I just wanted to bring it to the attention of the house.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PENSION PROVISIONS AND DISTRIBUTION OF FINES AND PENALTIES
speechtext: May I ask the minister what are the relations between the Department of Justice and the mounted police? Is the mounted police under the instructions and directions of the Department of Justice with regard to instituting prosecutions? My reason for asking the question is this: It sometimes appears as if the mounted police used entirely their own discretion as to what informations they should lay and what prosecutions they should commence, and on inquiry an intimation is given that the Department of Justice has nothing whatever to do with the matter. Is that the situation or does the minister consider himself as having control of the mounted police and as having the mounted police in aid of the civil power as vested in him for the purpose of prosecutions and the enforcement of law?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: EXTENSION OF PENSION PROVISIONS AND DISTRIBUTION OF FINES AND PENALTIES
speechtext:
Under the statute the Minister of Justice is described as the minister in control of the mounted police; that is the official title. But so far as prosecutions instituted by the mounted police during my term as Minister of Justice are concerned, I have not interfered with those prosecutions. I am referring to prosecutions involving rights of the crown, the revenues of the crown and the like, smuggling cases, all revenue cases. When a prosecution is instituted, it is instituted by an officer of the mounted police and in the vast majority of cases without my knowledge. That is the instruction which the commissioner has in regard to such cases. That pertains particularly to the three provinces of Ontaiio, Quebec and British Columbia 
in which the mounted police has no jurisdiction outside of government cases. But in all the other provinces, under agreements made with the provincial governments, the mounted police does perform the police duties of the whole province, and in those provinces it is more or less under the direction of the attorney general of the province concerned. I am not in any way consulted about the cases in those provinces. But in Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia in revenue cases, the action taken is taken on the initiative of the mounted police itself. Of course in the more important cases I am asked to nominate counsel for the conduct of the proceedings and in the majority of cases that is the first intimation I have that a prosecution is taking place. I have felt that it is not part of my duty to interfere in these prosecutions. I have time and again been requested by very able counsel, by the leading lawyers of this country, to intervene and to give them an opportunity of laying their case before me in order, I suppose, to allay or delay the prosecution or something of that kind, and I have refused to consider the question or to consult with them. Therefore to that extent in revenue cases the action taken is taken by the mounted police; they have control of the proceedings and they are very averse to any interference from any source whatever. Of course there are cases in which they do consult me, but not in regard to initial prosecution; they consult me in regard to the conduct of the case, the lawyers and the like.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PENSION PROVISIONS AND DISTRIBUTION OF FINES AND PENALTIES
speechtext:
I would like to call attention to an incident which happened in my constituency. On one occasion an officer of the mounted police came there in connection with a man in charge of a vessel. I do not know whether he gave this man instructions to put up his hands, but without any interference or provocation from the man, this mounted police official started to shoot all around. I do not know what took place afterwards, whether the question was taken before the courts and what was decided, but on that occasion the people were making complaints, such as have been made here to-day, that mounted police officers in our part of the country were taking the law into their own hands and administering it in a highhanded fashion. The Department of Justice, under whose administration the mounted police force is, ought to be careful to see that the instructions given to mounted police officers, not only when they are acting in their capacity as mounted police officials but at

Mounted Police Act
other times as well in those districts, are very strict so that similar incidents will not occur again.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: EXTENSION OF PENSION PROVISIONS AND DISTRIBUTION OF FINES AND PENALTIES
speechtext: If the hon. member will give me the names involved in the case he has just mentioned, I shall get a full report.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF PENSION PROVISIONS AND DISTRIBUTION OF FINES AND PENALTIES
speechtext: Following up my remarks and the reply made by the Minister of Justice, I am not talking about the matter of conducting prosecutions; what I am speaking of is the control of the minister in reference to instituting prosecutions. From some reports which have come to me, it seems that there have been cases in which the mounted police should refer to someone who understands the legal significance of the situation before the prosecution is actually commenced. In other words a report should be made to the minister in connection with revenue cases or any other cases under the dominion statutes, just as a report is made to the attorney general of a province or the crown prosecutor in a district, so that the attorney general or the crown prosecutor may give instructions and advice as to the person or persons against whom prosecution should be brought. What I am endeavouring to bring home to the minister is the idea that, it seems to me, he should not give up the control which the statute gives him over any part of the duties of the mounted police. He should not give them a blank cheque even to bring prosecutions without reference to him.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: EXTENSION OF PENSION PROVISIONS AND DISTRIBUTION OF FINES AND PENALTIES
speechtext:
I suppose if the rule as suggested by my hon. friend were adopted, it would apply to all cases. In many cases which one might call the more important ones, I have had occasion to discuss with the commissioner the case itself or perhaps the nature of the prosecution that took place, but I have never interfered with what he thought right to do in prosecuting this, that or the other person. The commissioner has of necessity had to consult in many instances some legal authority and in such cases he has consulted the law officers of my department and in some instances he has discussed the matter with me also. That does not apply to the general run of prosecutions. I suppose hundreds of them take place that I never hear about and no one in the Department of Justice hears about. I received a return to-day that in the last six months there have been forfeitures declared of cars and liquor amounting to $994,000. I never heard of those cases but the prosecutions have taken place. Those are conducted by the mounted police; but if serious matters arise such as the seizure of a
big vessel or a serious breach of the Customs Act. those matters would come to me through either the mounted police or the Department of National Revenue and in such cases we would advise. We do maintain general control of the mounted police, but "minister in control," as I think my predecessor will inform the house too, really means the person to represent the force in parliament, to see that the necessary supply is voted, to obtain any amendments that may be necessary to the law, and to have general charge of the force. So far as the internal economy of the force goes, I do not intermeddle at all. For instance, appointments, promotions and the, like come before me as a matter of form for, confirmation, but I leave these things entirely to the commissioner whom I believe to be, well qualified to manage the force. In legal matters in .more important cases consultations take place, but thousands o*f prosecutions art never heard of by the department.

All I want to impress
upon the minister is that I submit that he should not, and I take it from his statement t-hait he does not, treat- the matter of control which is given by the statute as a purely formal or administrative matter. The police, after all, are like the military, used in aid of the civil power, represented in the person and office of the minister and for them he is responsible to parliament.
While I am on my feet, if I may refer to section 4, since we have discussed it-

Hon. members who have preceded me have spoken of the objection to this legislation on the ground that it seemed to put the police on the basis of a military force. The minister states that the police are not a military force, and of course we know that legally they are not. Nevertheless 1 submit that the explanation that appears on the opposite page would indicate that the police have the idea that they should be treated as on all fours with the permanent military forces of Canada as far as remuneration, pay and allowances are concerned. I submit that the adoption of that principle in connection with the administration of justice in Canada is dangerous, and that it is no sufficient reason for increasing pensions to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police that it happens that such and such a pension may be allowed to the military forces of Canada. The police are a civil force, their pensions are

more properly approximated to the pensions of civil servants. That is the first point.
The second is, I submit that at this time when we are trying to soften a little the blows which the taxpayer is receiving, we should not rush to add further pension allowances or bonuses to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, particularly when those who would benefit by this provision are men who have entered the service under a contract which did not contain any such provision; in other words that this is a straight bonus added to pay, there is no contractual obligation of any kind, and no moral obligation, I take it, to make these payments. speechtext:
The minister pointed out that British Columbia is one of the provinces that maintain a provincial police force and in that province the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are not in charge. The municipal police and the provincial police there I think are fairly competent. My reason for rising at this time is to draw the attention of the minister to what I call a racket that has been going on in British Columbia in the municipality of Richmond this last year under the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I think this is a proper time to call the matter to his attention, because if it is allowed to go on it is going to be very serious for the people and residents out in that province. Having had some municipal experience, I fully realize that there are cases in which one has to hire a certain type of person if the object is to catch someone who is selling liquor for instance or otherwise breaking the law. But we had in the municipality of Richmond last year men engaged by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police who deliberately went out and framed people. It was not a case of going out and asking a man if they could get a drink from him, it was a case of going and saying to him, "Would you like to make some money? If so I will provide you with some liquor." If the man fell for this story then in a short time the Royal Canadian Mounted Police came along and picked him up.
Let me lay this case also before the minister: this man has an electrical store in New Westminster. One morning there walked into his store a man with a small radio, saying he would like to exchange it for another radio. After some discussion he took another radio costing a little more and turned in this small radio in exchange. Half an hour later two Royal Canadian Mounted Policemen


Mounted Police Act
walked in and arrested that man for having a radio that was smuggled into the country. Where is that going to land' us if men like these are let loose on the country? In the liquor case also the man was hired by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and no action was taken even when it was drawn to the attention of the officers that the man they were engaging was a fugitive from justice in New Zealand and should not be in this country at all. When the police of Richmond endeavoured to get some information they found themselves blocked by the Immigration department officers, who said, No, we cannot give any information because we are a little afraid of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police; if we say or do anything we might come under their displeasure. It seems to me that all a man has to do if he commits some crime is to get hired by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and he will be immune. These matters are serious. The municipal police are endeavouring to and do enforce the law, the provincial police the same, and in an efficient manner and I do not think it is the duty of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to hire men to go through the country and deliberately ask men if they would like to make some money, and if they ask. How? Oh well, we will supply you with a little liquor and the bottles and the labels. This thing has been going on for some considerable time.
I have in my hand a court record. It has to do with a case in which a man was picked up by the municipal police and charged with selling liquor. When he was in the witness box the judge called him a blatant and unrepentant liar, and he was in the employ of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. As one who has looked into the matter I say that if this thing is not stopped and if men hired by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police can go around the country, frame you and report the matter to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police who come along shortly after and pick you up the lives of people will not be safe. I should like the minister to take serious note of this, also to tell the house if any of the moiety was paid to these men, and what moiety they receive.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS

speechtext:
Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 15, to amend the Canadian Farm Loan Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Smith (Cumberland) in the chair.
On the short title.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the resolution preceding this bill was 'before the house, from the acclaim with which it was accepted I was under the impression that I
was attending a meeting of the farmers of Canada rather than a meeting of the House of Commons.
I Should like to refer to some of the remarks that were made by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Willis) who, if I remember correctly, complained about the difficulty in procuring loans. His complaint was, I think, that the officers of the board either were using too much discretion or that they did not have sufficient authority to loan money in certain areas in the district which he represented. Remarks from members on all sides of the house who supported the resolution on that occasion led me to believe that their impression was that these moneys were not so much to be loaned on an economic and sound basis as they were to be put into the bands of the farmers on a basis which was probably not sufficiently sound to encourage the investment of private capital. The hon. member for Souris in his remarks, critical I may say of the administration of the farm loan board, questioned their judgment, and my impression, from the remarks of other hon. members was that probably it is more a question of government policy whether the farm loan board should loan money in certain areas and as to the conditions under which it should 'be loaned. I would like very much for the minister to state to the house as definitely as he can his opinion as to the soundness that is going to be required ^ loaning of this money. In other words, are-we through this measure going to give money where it is not always economically sound to-loan it? Are we going to put it into the" hands of the farmers of this country as a matter of national policy? While I quite agree that that might be a desirable policy I am not discussing that at the moment, but I think we should know at this time what the policy of the government is going to be and what instructions are to be given to the farm loan board. Are they to take into con* sideration the necessities of the situation in so far as the development of agriculture is concerned, or are they to be a farm loan board, and not a farm gift board? I would like the minister to give us some assurance of what we may expect in this regard.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the discussion when I moved the resolution and later in committee on the resolution itself covered a wide field, and I thought I had endeavoured to make it clear that the purpose of the board would be to deal with each individual case on its merits, the main purpose and

Farm Loan Act

object being to assist preferably the deserving and worthy farmer; or I might make it stronger than that and say, the farmer who after having received a loan is likely to succeed upon the farm.
The criticism that my hon. friend referred to which came from the hon. member for Souris was applicable to the policy which had been pursued through the provincial board, and my hon. friend will bear in mind that hereafter there will be no provincial boards. But even in the case of the provincial boards, as I understand it there were no areas proscribed. Naturally one would think that a prudent man would scrutinize with extreme care an inquiry for a loan in an area where crop failure had covered a period of years. But I do think that there the long view would have to be taken, and that even in those areas where, covering a period of many years, there had been on the whole good crops, the man himself being a good farmer and a good moral risk, there would be no reason why in a case of that character there should not be a reasonable degree of latitude on the part of the farm loan board. In other words, it goes without saying that the first class risk, the highest class risk in the ordinary course of events would foe taken care of either by individuals or by loan companies in the loaning business. It does not by any means follow that the government must be called upon to take second and third class risks, but I do say that the government would be justified, having in mind the desirability of assisting the farmer and keeping him on the land, in taking a wider measure of risk than would be taken in the case of an individual motivated solely by the desire to invest his money profitably. I do not know whether I have covered the question put by my hon. friend; if not, I shall be glad to endeavour to answer any supplementary questions which he might wish to ask.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I thank the minister
for his remarks, and I think we are getting close to the point I wish to have covered. Before I make any further remarks however, I should like the minister to answer this question. Is it the policy of the government that all risks must in the past have been high class risks?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I could not answer that
by a direct yes or no. The farm loan board has been in operation a number of years and has endeavoured to conduct its operations prudently. In fact, the criticism has been that it has conducted its operations too prudently; we have heard such criticism in 
the course of this debate. If there is any criticism against the operations of the board it is that they have been too careful in their loaning operations.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I am rather anxious to
have this point cleared up, because although the minister stated that the criticism of the hon. member for Souris was with reference to the provincial board, I have a distinct recollection that he did also make some reference to the board as it exists in Ottawa; and I believe he went so far as to suggest that there should be changes and removals. It is for that reason that I should like to have that point cleared up. The minister pointed out to us that in the loaning of money to high class risks, there was probably even to-day private money available for the purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: For the highest class.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Yes; private capital is
available for that to-day. Consequently, if for that highest class risk money is available, then the government will have for their loans the high class or the questionable risk, and I think all members should know definitely, what the policy of the government is to be. If we are making this a farm relief act we should know it; if it is a farm loan act we should know that also. Are we loaning money or relieving farmers? Are we going to make loans on high class risks or are we going to give the board instructions that now they may consider the questionable risk on the basis indicated by the minister, that the value of equity is not to be the only consideration? I think he is justified in taking that view. In the past we have prided ourselves on such a thing as a man establishing credit, and that is something which I think should exist in this measure. But it is absolutely important to the people of Canada to know how this board is going to function. Is it going to function as a distinctly farm loan board or are we to take the question of risks into consideration and to that extent have the act function as a farm relief measure?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
It goes without saying
that when this act was passed four or five or six years ago the board was established not because the government desired to go into the money lending business but because there was felt to be a need at that time for this type of legislation. I pointed that out in my remarks during the discussion of the resolution.

Farm Loan Act

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: And because we have the balance of power.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
It is intended that the
business should be conducted as a farm loan business and not as a relief undertaking. But at the same time, every hon. member knows quite well that the object in mind with the old government, as it is with this government and would be with any government, the main object in mind was to lend assistance to the agricultural interests who would be denied an opportunity of getting loans were it not for this act. The need has become greater during the last two or three years, for reasons which are obvious. I do not know that I can say anything more. I think the act will have to be administered with a reasonable degree of prudence, but no government would be wise to allow the board to operate in such a negligent way as to throw its money away. Care will have to be exercised; but having in mind the main object, namely, to assist the worthy farmer who is likely to succeed, certainly a reasonable degree of latitude ought to be allowed.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: The remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver Burrard (Mr. Hanbury) give rise to a point in regard to which there may be misapprehension as to the credit of the farmers themselves. Some of the statements made on the resolution before the house the other day, so far as Ontario is concerned at any rate, might seriously impair the chances of the farmers of even securing loans under t'he Canadian Farm Loan Act. I think much can be said in favour of taking into consideration the element of personal credit as well as that of land values, as mentioned. I agree with the hon. minister and appreciate the attitude he has taken. In Ontario we are in an even more difficult position than I indicated the other day-

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: Why bring that up?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Well, the reason I bring it up is the fact that we have had in that province for a period of over twelve years what is known as the Ontario agricultural development board which I think all hon. members will agree has been functioning not especially with a view to relief but for the assistance of the farmers throughout that province during that time. When the government changed last June, as governments often do, we had 900 applications that had been passed, inspected and approved of by the board, mortgages prepared and in many cases registered. For months these farmers waited daily for their
money and 500 more in respect of which inspection fees had been paid, many of the applicants not having had their fees refunded, daily expected results. But the practice of a policy covering a period of twelve years was immediately and completely reversed. I mention that fact at this stage as there might be some misapprehension with regard to the credit of the farmers of Ontario and the soundness of that policy as it had been carried out. I say this for the benefit of those who will be administering this act, so that the chances of the farmers of Ontario to secure loans under this legislation will not be too seriously impaired. Everyone will agree I think that when a policy has been in operation for twelve years, involving a sum of over $50,000,000, so far as farm mortgage loaning is concerned, it is almost entirely removed from private corporations or individuals. The farmers therefore have little recourse other than to apply to the government, which they have been doing.
The other day some statements were made that reflect upon the soundness of that policy and might have an adverse effect upon the continuance of loaning to the farmers. I did not interrupt the hon. member for Fron-tenac-Addington (Mr. Campbell) when he was speaking as there is a time-honoured custom that when an hon. member is making his maiden speech, no matter what ridiculous statements he may make or how excited he may get, we should not interrupt. He made a very spectacular statement; he said:
I want to make it clear to all hon. members that prior to the month of May the interest rate on farm loan mortgages in Ontario stood at six per cent. During the election campaign, in which I had the privilege of taking an active interest-
We are quite aware of that.

it was announced that that rate would' be lowered to five and a half per cent and it was cut to five per cent during the heat of the election.
As a matter of fact, I might inform the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington in all kindness, while his speech was fine in form, it was somewhat ridiculous in fact. The interest rate on loans in Ontario has not been six per cent for almost ten years. Some years ago the late Ferguson government reduced the rate from six to five and a half per cent. During the last session of the Ontario legislature the matter was discussed and debated there on several occasions and prior to the last election the rate was reduced from five and a half to five per cent. Before the heat of the election, as spoken of by
Farm Loan Act

the hon. member, the rate was reduced and became effective at five per cent, as every hon. member from Ontario knows, weeks before the election. In the heat of the election I think it was stated that if the then government were returned, they would reduce the interest rate to a lower figure. Since that time another government has been in power and immediately on assuming office it discontinued that policy entirely. The fourteen hundred farmers to whom I have referred waited daily for some relief, some assurance, something definite to know whether they would be compelled to go to private individuals or mortgage companies in order to secure the money for which they had applied and to accept the loans in connection with which inspections had been made and which the old board had passed.
I do not wish to delay the committee on this bill, but the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington further stated:
When the new provincial government took office they made an investigation to find out just how the agricultural development board stood, and they discovered that some $55,000,000 of the people's money had been loaned throughout Ontario. One unfortunate experience -was that many loans had been made, not for the purpose of allowing a farmer to permit his son to purchase a farm and some new stock and start up in business, or for the farmer to improve his farm, by building a new barn or house, but rather at the instance of influential people, supporters of the late government.
I doubt if there is an hon. member from Ontario who can give one instance where political influence had any bearing. He says further:
That is a serious statement to make.
It is a serious statement to make when he follows it with the further statement that the provincial government have been making loans since. He stated that in November of last year some seventy-two loans were made, amounting to about $140,000. I challenge him to show a single loan that has been made on the initiative of the provincial government, and rather than boasting of the seventy-two loans that he says were made, he should apologize because there are only seventy-two out of one thousand four hundred, nine hundred of which were approved by the board. There are still more than eight hundred farmers whose loans have been approved and who are still waiting for some advance.
The hon. member for West Elgin also made his maiden effort and I did not wish to interrupt him, but his statements were no less

reckless, though his speech was not quite so long as that of the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington. He said:
In reference to that board, what were the conditions the present government found when they assumed office? They found stacks of applications that had been passed' by the Henry government.
This statement is rather conspicuous merely as an insinuation that he had some inside information and it was due to political influence they had been passing the loans. As regards that feature of the matter I wish to point out to the committee that I have secured the last report of the Ontario agricultural development board and the ridiculousness of these statements is shown by the fact that in 1933, the previous year, that board had made seven hundred and forty-two fewer loans than they did in 1932, and for the first eight months of 1934 they loaned $1,600,000 less than they did in 1933, so that the loans that were being made in Ontario were evidently being lessened every year.
Much has been said with reference to the maladministration of the Ontario agricultural development board as an excuse for not helping the farmer, but may I point out that while it has been said that this board has been recklessly handled, they had a surplus in administration costs and carrying charges of $769,458.67, as shown in the report to which I refer. I have failed to see why we should apologize for the actions of the former provincial government in that regard. It was further pointed out by the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Mills) that 18,000 Ontario farmers, who were evidently friends of the government, had been loaned $51,000,000 and that if those loans were liquidated to-day, they would not be worth $15,000,000. This is a point I wish to emphasize because it reflects upon the credit of the farmers of Ontario, and upon the soundness of their land holdings and it might impair the possibility of their securing loans from the duly established board under the amended act that is now before the house. I think every hon. member will agree that the statement made by my hon. friend is a ridiculous one. I ask, in all kindness to him is a new member, how he ever reached that figure. There is another time-honoured custom in this house that a member should be careful not to make statements without giving them sound thought and preparation. I see some hon. members smile and after listening to him yesterday I think I know why. If one made throughout Ontario the inspection that would be necessary to be able to make that type of statement, I will leave

Farm Loan Act
it to any hon. member if he would consider that a reasonable assumption, because it is a most ridiculous one. In the first place the Ontario agricultural development board's policy has been for twelve years not to loan more than fifty per cent of the farm value. It is very true, with arrears of interest, that might in years such as those through which we have passed, accumulate an obligation more than fifty per cent. The value in many cases was the value before the war, because inflated values of war time were not taken into very much account by the average inspector. In my local district as in many other parts of Ontario one hundred acre farms were valued at from S8,000 to $12,000 long before the great war. These 18.000 loans in Ontario average only $2,200 each. In exceptional circumstances they might be as high as $4,000. If this is a reasonable assumption then the insinuation seems to be that farms that were originally worth $8,000 in Ontario are to-day only worth $1,800, and farms formerly worth $4,500 are now assumed to be worth $900, and farms formerly worth $2,000 the newly elected hon. member would say are worth only $450. I wish to impress on the committee that the soundness of Ontario farm values is not so badly impaired as is suggested. If $36,000,000 of the $51,000,000 that has been loaned will be lost, as suggested, then it would be our duty not to support the second reading of this bill. In that case our agricultural situation would be next to hopeless. I do not know why that statement should be made other than to justify those who have neglected, inexcusably neglected their obligation at a time that has been very critical for the farmers of Ontario. The policy of securing money from the board has been established and now when appeal is made to private individuals applicants are asked why they do not get it from the government.
I make this statement in an endeavour to show as clearly as I can a true picture of the farm loan situation in Ontario. I wish to urge upon the minister on behalf not only of the farmers of Ontario but those of every part of the country that he should secure money for the farmers, as I feel satisfied he will, at the lowest possible interest rate. I know every hon. member who is interested in agriculture, as we all are, appreciates the fact that the farmers have had a difficult time in recent years and that the prices of many things they have had to buy have not fallen to the same degree as the prices of what they produce, so I think it is necessary for the economic soundness of the country that we should have as low a rate of interest as it is possible for the
government to give in view of the cost of long term bonds, their carrying charges and the necessary reserves.
In Ontario our situation, is a little different, for we have never had the Canadian Farm Loan Act in operation in Ontario. Whether it was owing to the struggle for power or for whatever reason, all parties in Ontario said they were in favour of lower interest rates. The Minister of Agriculture in Ontario not long ago stated emphatically that no matter what rate this government charged under this new Farm Loan Act, the farmers of Ontario will not have to pay more than four per cent, and the balance, if any, will be paid by the province.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I hear an hon. member say
"Hear, hear," and I am quite in agreement with him; and I am very glad that the farmers of Ontario will in no event have to pay more than four per cent in the future. May I also remind the committee that Ontario has given loans at one per cent less than the Dominion board for some time, and that is all the more justification for the remarks I have made as to the soundness of Ontario agriculture. I have heard the former Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) in this house and others say that the risks in Ontario have not been as great as in some other provinces, and probably that is the reason why when the late government was in power and since the Canadian Farm Loan Act was put into effect in 1927, farmers in Ontario enjoyed this one per cent advantage. The Ontario agricultural development board were making loans in Ontario at one per cent less at all times than the dominion government, and for a short time one and a half per cent less. So even if the rate in the future should be left at five per cent the Ontario farmers will still enjoy a one per cent advantage, according to the statement made by the present government of Ontario. I have not too much faith in that government but I must commend them for that statement; I hope they will keep their word. So, whether or not this government see fit to lower their rate below four per cent, which I doubt is possible, I am not particularly concerned about their action, as to the rate of interest, because it Is mot a question of what the farmer in Ontario will have to pay, it is a question of who will have to pay the difference.
I do not wish to keep the committee longer, except to say that I think the farmers of Ontario during the last three or four years have shown what they can accomplish and to emphasize the fact to which I have already
Farm Loan Act

referred that loans have not been increasing as hon. members have said, for we had 742 less in 1933 than in 1932, and they loaned $1,600,000 leas in the first eight months of 1934, although that was prior to an ejection. Therefore I think it is impossible for anyone to claim that loans were made for political purposes, or to doubt the soundness of the agricultural situation in Ontario which by all the signs of the times is at least slightly and gradually improving.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
The point I wish to
bring to the attention of the minister has already been mentioned. It is this, that up to the present there certainly have been areas absolutely excluded from any benefit of the farm loan board. The area in which I live is one of them. When a farmer applies to that board for a loan he is told that no loans are being considered in that whole district. They do not ask him what his prospects are, or his assets, or inquire into his ability or anything. I have many letters to that effect. I should like the minister to give us some assurance that these individual cases will be decided on their merits rather than all come under one general rule.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I have on a number of
occasions endeavoured to make it very clear that each case would be considered on its individual merits, irrespective of the location of the area. It may be that the hon. member was not in the house on those occasions, and I am very happy indeed to repeat that assurance to him.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I am glad that the finance
minister has made that statement so clearly and frequently; I think it ought to have been impressed on the house by this time, that in future loans will be considered on their merits. I listened with much interest to the speech of the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Willis), I do not always agree with him but I felt on that occasion that he was stating a very real grievance. The hon. member for Souris represents a district in Manitoba which more than any other perhaps has suffered from the drought. He pointed out, very correctly, that in that district there are large areas which in the past have produced enormous wealth, districts where they have the finest equipment and buildings, and there is no reason why many of those men should be refused a loan. I had a similar grievance, for the matter was brought to my attention that loans were being refused in what was spoken of as the dried-out area. I made a protest myself to

the Manitoba authorities and also to the dominion head office, and I got word from Doctor MacLean that it was not the policy of the central office to rule out the dried-out areas altogether, but rather that cases would be considered on their individual merits. I would like to point out and emphasize the fact that while some of these districts, including part of my own territory, have suffered from drought for the last two years, that is one of the very finest countries under the sun. There is no reason why there should be any discrimination against a section of the country because, for a period of two or three years, there has been drought in that district. There are men with well established and well equipped farms who need just a little help to tide them over. We have all confidence in that country; we believe rain will come again, and that is all we need in order to produce a large amount of wealth in the future. So I say again that I am glad the minister has made the statement that each case will be decided upon its own merits.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I was very glad to hear the statement of the minister in regard to the point raised by the hon. member for Medicine Hat. Undoubtedly in the past some of the provincial boards have taken the attitude that they would not consider applications from certain areas. I have gone into those areas and found farmers making a decided success. It is true that they were living in so called drought areas, which had been abandoned by a good many farmers, but these men knew how to make a living there; they were making good, and I think in many cases were catching up with their liabilities. So it seemed to me a wrong attitude on the part of a provincial board to practically tell a man that he lived in an area from which they would not even consider applications for loans.
I just want to add at this time, taking into consideration the condition of agriculture and the terrible time it has gone through, the government should make provision for the granting of credit under the farm loan board at a rate of four per cent, with any cost above that assumed by the Dominion of Canada. I am not sure, but perhaps the hon. member for Yancouver-Burrard will object to that. A few moments ago he spoke of first class farm loans, but many loans that were considered first class a few years ago now are far from that. That is due to conditions altogether beyond the control of the farmers. The reason for this condition has been the drop in the price level of the things the farmer produces. It might be

Farm Loan Act
worth while telling this committee once more the drop that has taken place in the cash income of the farmers of Canada. These figures were given in connection with a chart that recently appeared in the monthly letter of one of our Canadian banks. In 1926 the cash income of the farmers of Canada was
8941.000.	000. In 1932 it had fallen to
8396.000.	000, which was only 42 per cent of the 1926 income. It is quite evident that interest could not be paid out of a net income that had been reduced to that extent. In 1928 the income was 81,113,000,000, so there was a drop from 1928 to 1932 of 64 per cent, or in other words the cash income of the farmers of Canada in 1932 was only 36 per cent of the income in 1928.
In reality the solution of the farm credit problem is to restore the price level of farm products. No matter what we may do for the farmers in the way of credit facilities, if we do not do something to raise the price level of farm products we cannot get a satisfactory credit system. At the present time the price level is improving, but as yet it is not at a point which will allow the farmers to carry their present burden of indebtedness. The loan value of our farms is largely determined by the rate of interest charged on farm loans, as the amount of loan that a farm can carry and pay interest on is determined as much by the rate of interest as by the size of the loan. I believe the rate of interest is the important thing for us to consider in connection with this act, and without taking up more of the time of the committee I want to urge on the minister that the government assume any necessary costs of administration and so forth, so that loans may be made under this act at a rate of not more than four per cent per annum.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
When the resolution which preceded this bill was under consideration the other evening the hon. member for Laprairie-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) is reported as having said:
I have tried to find a reason why the government is bringing down this legislation at this late hour. I have asked myself: Is it because they have tried that other legislation called the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act which they passed last year, and which as a matter of fact has completely destroyed the credit of the farmer of eastern Canada?
I am reported as having said:
It was all destroyed before that law was passed.
I do not rise to withdraw a single word of that affirmation, but it certainly calls for some explanation which I could not give on that occasion. In the past, and even to-day,
the farming population of Quebec have had the best credit of the whole community. They were considered, as I am sure they are considered to-day, honest as a class. There are exceptions in all classes, but I think they had and still have the reputation of being first class credit risks.
When I made that declaration I wanted to point out that the act referred to by the hon. member had not destroyed the credit of the farmer, but that his credit had been destroyed, so far as that could be done legally, by previous measures passed by the provincial government of Quebec. One of the causes of the impairment of the farmers' credit is the number of preferred debts that in Quebec have precedence over the first mortgage. Being an ordinary layman I cannot speak as a lawyer, but I am told by persons who should know that we have almost twice as many of these preferred debts as any other province in Canada. I should like to enumerate some of them. First there are the legal costs. I suppose they are preferred in every province, but I should like to point out that in Quebec they are certainly not lower and I think probably they are higher than in any other province of the dominion. Funeral costs are preferred before the first mortgage is paid, together with the expenses of the last sickness, and the cost of ploughing and seeding for the current or the last season. Then, it is only fair that the taxes should be paid. The cost of labour, material and the bill of the contractor for any buildings erected on the property or on the farm are paid before the first mortgage is considered and the wages of servants are paid. As hon. members will see, this is a long list of preferred bills which in many cases may take up half the value of the mortgaged property. In this way the credit of the farmer is further decreased. In making these observations I am not being critical; I do not say the measures are no good or do not serve any useful purpose. I simply wish to establish my contention that even before the act to which reference has been made was passed the credit of the farmer was destroyed beyond repair. Certainly his credit was very much decreased when the moratorium on mortgages was passed tow or three years ago by the legislature of the province of Quebec. It was further decreased when legislation was passed exempting from seizure certain stock, implements and cattle-going as high as ten cows-a team of horses and a complete stock of farm implements. I am not criticizing this law, but I do say it had the effect of decreasing or impairing the farmer's credit, when the lending
Farm Loan Act

party was considering lending money on first mortgage. The moratorium is still in effect in the province of Quebec; if interest and taxes are paid, no mortgage can be collected.
Then, there is a further factor which has had something to do with impairing the credit of the farmers, namely the privileges given to different firms selling on terms. As a layman I thought this matter was within the competence of the federal parliament, but after consulting able lawyers I was told it was a matter which had to do with civil rights, and that there could be no doubt where the jurisdiction rested. In my opinion in the last few years probably more than at any other time these privileges have done a great deal to destroy the credit of the farmer. In the province of Quebec companies selling on terms have the privilege of remaining the owners of the property sold. I do not complain about that, but when a purchaser defaults on one or more payments the selling company has the privilege of taking possession of the property. Again I do not find fault. The fault I find is this: The company repossess the article in question, whether it be an automobile or something else, and may proceed to make repairs which cost anywhere from $300 to S500. Then they sail the repossessed article for whatever figure they can get, provided the original purchaser is in fairly good financial condition, although possibly not able to make his payments. Having sold the article they may claim the balance from the original owner. In my opinion this process more than any other factor has been responsible for the impairment of the credit of the farmers. Hon. members are familiar with the tactics of what we term high pressure salesmen, and we realize that the poor farmer who is not accustomed to discussions and arguments is not proof against the sales talk. The salesman ascertains before he visits the farmer if the person he is visiting is financially responsible. In many cases these salesmen have sold to farmers against their will and against their own interests. Hon. members know' how many farm implements, sewing machines and automobiles have been sold to farmers who, when the agent visited them for the first time, had no intention of buying. I say such companies should have to make a choice, when they repossess an article-

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am afraid
I cannot congratulate the minister upon this legislation. Like the unemployment insurance bill and most of the social legislation we hear so much about nowadays, it will have the effect only of raising the hopes of the needy and then dashing them to the ground. The farm loan act was first passed in 1927, and $15,000,000 was placed at its disposal. In seven years of operation the board had loaned only $9,000,000. Last year the amount available to the board was increased to $40,000,000, and I believe at this time they have loaned out $15,000,000. Now we propose to increase the amount available to $90,000,000, and I venture to say w'hen we come back next year less than half of it will have been loaned. It is not the amount of money you have to lend that counts, but the amount that you are willing to lend. How are the loans to be made? On appraisal. Very well, but who is going to benefit by it? Only the very best and the very worst farmers. The farmer who is in such good shape that his debts do not amount to very much will have no trouble in going to the board and getting money at five per cent with which to pay off the debts on which he is now paying seven or eight per cent. In that way they skim off the cream of the mortgage business. On the other hand, the farmer who is in such desperate shape that his creditors have no hope of getting anything out of him anyway will be able to go to his creditors and make this kind of compromise with them. They will say: We will give you a clear receipt for whatever amount you can get out of the farm loan board. They will use every influence they can to get all they can out of the board so that they can get that much of what is owing to them, and then they will leave the board to deal with the worst class of farmers.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: I should like to support the statement made by the hon. member for Vegreville on behalf of men who I think should be able to get loans but who have been turned down. I have in mind an old man who has a good farm. He put his boys on it and went himself to the city to give his younger children a better education. He bought a house in the city with a mortgage on it, but on account of the serious conditions of the times he is not able to get sufficient return from his farm to pay off the interest on the mortgage or even to pay his taxes. He made application for a loan but was turned down, on the ground I suppose that 'he was not living on the farm. This man has lived on the farm for fifty years, and has made good on it up to recent years. He is really a farmer. The farm is his only means of getting a living, but his application was turned down because he was not actually living on the farm, I suppose, although his boys' are there. I hope the new act will have a clause that will enable such men, even if they are not living on the farm, to get a loan when they are really dependent on the farm. This man is over seventy years of age. He is not in a position to get an old age -pension because of his farm, and for the same reason he cannot go on relief, nor can he get relief from the farm loan board.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Last year when we were discussing the debt adjustment act we were given the assurance that in many cases where debts were composed there was a strong probability of the debtor being able to rearrange his mortgage indebtedness and thereby be in a position in somes cases to pay off the total of his indebtedness by a new loan secured from the farm loan board. I think I am safe in making the assertion that with at least eighty per cent of our farmers to-day the difficulty is not so much with their floating indebtedness, although that is an important factor, as with the accumulated arrears of interest that are added to the principal of his loan. I must frankly admit that the accumulation of interest added to the
Farm, Loan Act

principal makes the total indebtedness in many cases beyond the actual selling value of the farm at to-day's prices, and the result was of course that no relief could be afforded in such cases by the farm loan board.
I am well aware, too, that the object of the farm loan board at its inception was not so much to lend large sums of money, not even up to the maximum, as to give the small farmer, the one who perhaps had the most difficulty in securing a loan, the opportunity to secure a very moderate loan. I think that policy was fairly well carried out. I believe also that the board did discriminate to some extent where larger loans were required. I am not speaking of loans up to the maximum. But this situation has arisen-I will give a hypothetical case. A debtor makes application to the registrar and gets a substantial reduction in his floating indebtedness, but when it comes to a question of adjustment with the company which holds the mortgage on present day values, there is great reluctance on the part of the farm loan board to lend the money. I am not criticizing that attitude. I admit that if the farm were sold at present day prices it would not perhaps bring the mortgage indebtedness accrued against it. But that resulted in a sort of impasse in our province in which the mortgage companies took the ground that they were not forced to compose the indebtedness unless they were to be paid off. I want to convey to the minister the difficulty of this situation. It usually meant that that loan was not settled but remained in abeyance. What I want to know is this. Have the debt adjustment board authority to force the mortgage company to take a reduction of their loan unless they are in a position to liquidate that loan and pay it off in cash? And even if they are in a position to do so, have the board authority to reduce the indebtedness of the mortgage and accrued interest?
